reconcile.connective: Defenders count Jehoiachin's three-month vassal reign as too slight to register, so Jeremiah's word that Jehoiakim would have none on David's throne stands without conflict.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the plain conflict: 2 Kings says Jehoiakim's son Jehoiachin reigned in his stead, yet Jeremiah swore Jehoiakim would have no one to sit on David's throne.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999– )

excerpts.excerpt_text: The very brief reign of this prince, which lasted only three months, during which he was a humble vassal of the Assyrians, is scarcely deserving to be taken into account, and therefore is in no way contradictory to the prophetic menace denounced against his father (Jer 36:30).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names the contradiction explicitly and dissolves it: Jehoiachin's three-month vassal reign is too slight to count, so it does not falsify Jeremiah's word that Jehoiakim would have none on the throne. The squarest of the harmonizing voices (Gill, Clarke, K&D say the same). Parity-capped to this single strongest excerpt on a discrepancy_first row.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the Jehoiakim succession under the harmonizing tradition that a three-month vassal reign ending in deportation is not a true sitting upon David's throne.

link.title: Jeremiah 36:30 — How can this verse say Jehoiakim shall have no one to sit on the throne when his son reigned after him?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment arguing the Hebrew 'sit on the throne' connotes a permanent enthronement that Jehoiachin's three-month reign never achieved.
